Title: Can a deal 1-2-2 be legal at the beginning of the game?

Messages.Author: Ector
Messages.Body:
Can a player make a deal with two other players on the 5-player table
to split the table 1-2-2 if that player is going to gain only one VP
from the deal? (I mean, would he violate PTW this way?) Can he propose
the deal on the first turn of the game?
Does the player gaining only 1VP from the deal need to prove his
inability of getting more than 1VP? What about the players gaining
2VPs?

Thanks in advance,
Ector

Messages.Author: LSJ
Messages.Body:
Ector wrote:
> Can a player make a deal with two other players on the 5-player table
> to split the table 1-2-2 if that player is going to gain only one VP
> from the deal? (I mean, would he violate PTW this way?) Can he propose

It would if it does violate PTW. That is, if he has some way to get more
than 1 VP, then working toward a 1VP finish is not PTW.

If it doesn't (he has no way to reasonably get more than 1 VP), then it
doesn't violate PTW.

> the deal on the first turn of the game?

Unlikely, since it would be nearly impossible to get into a position where
he could not have some other way to get more VPs.

> Does the player gaining only 1VP from the deal need to prove his
> inability of getting more than 1VP? What about the players gaining
> 2VPs?

No one need prove anything -- if there's a question, call the judge
in to evaluate the game state and render a judgment. You can offer
whatever advice ("proof") you like to the judge, but the judge
ultimately relies on his judgment (and likewise, the judge need
not "prove" anything, either).

--

Messages.Author: Hardy Range
Messages.Body:
Ector wrote:
> Can a player make a deal with two other players on the 5-player table
> to split the table 1-2-2 if that player is going to gain only one VP
> from the deal?

Yes, if the current game state allows this (i.e, he cannot hope to get
a GW or more than 1 VP otherwise).

> (I mean, would he violate PTW this way?)

This depends on the current state of the game.
If he cannot win the game, he has to maximize his VPs.

> Can he propose
> the deal on the first turn of the game?

At the start of the turn: No, since there is no game state that would
prevent him from winning or getting more than 1 VP.
At the end of the turn (i.e., after some cards have been played or
vampires have been influenced out): Depends on the current state of the
game.

And note that both players going for just 2 VP also can only accept
that deal if they have no way to win in the current state of the game.

> Does the player gaining only 1VP from the deal need to prove his
> inability of getting more than 1VP? What about the players gaining
> 2VPs?

The judge decides what the current game state does or does not allow.
If he needs "proof" (i.e., a more informed basis for his personal
opinion), he is free to get his information from whatever sources he
needs (e.g., looking through a player's library, or have the players
explain their reasoning).

Regards,

Hardy Range

The technical answer (as already provided) is maybe. The practical
answer is no. There is virtually no way for a player to convince the
judge that he has no way of winning on the first turn of the game. The
only way it would be even close to reasonable might be if he has
influenced out several weenies and his prey has Aranthebes. But I
would think that a reasonable judge would insist that he try to burn
Aranthebes, or try to get someone else to do it for him. Further, it's
not inconceivable that he has larger vampires in the crypt, or
something else he can do besides bleed. I would think any reasonable
judge would say, "just play the stupid game". Deals are all fine and
good and are an important part of the game, but there's a point where
deal-making gets ridiculous.

>> than 1 VP, then working toward a 1VP finish is not PTW.
>
>> If it doesn't (he has no way to reasonably get more than 1 VP), then it
>> doesn't violate PTW.
> AFAIK, *every* player has some way to oust all other players - at
> least, the probability of this is greater than zero. Does this mean
> that ALL table-splitting deals are illegal?

Usually on the first turn of the game they are illegal, correct.

Of course, time goes by, turns are taken, decisions are made, and
the state of the game frequently changes such that one or more players
can no longer reaonably hope for more than one or two VP and have no
realistic chance to win the game. At such a point, a table splitting
deal might be legal.

> Anyway, how can a judge determine the EXACT number of VPs any player
> can get? When a player wants to deal for 1 VP, somebody would call a
> judge... and the judge should determine the minimal number he could
> deal for, doesn't he?

Yep. That's how it works. As for the "how can a judge determine the
exact number of VP" question, sometimes it's easy to make a few common
sense observations and have a good idea, sometimes it's hard. If it's
really hard to see how a player is limited to fewer victory points than
what it takes to currently win the game, the judge probably should
determine that he can still win - and therefore he cannot deal to let
another player win.

> As I said, SOME way to get more VPs always exist - an extremely bad
> draw for all opponents, for instance. But why do I have to prohibit a
> player from getting 1VP if the player thinks that it would be the best
> way for him?

Because the rules don't allow it. The rules also don't allow switching
cards in your deck between game even if a player thinks that it would be
the best way for him. What are you confused about?

> Are table-splitting deals really possible, then?

Of course they are. The game has to have progressed to a point where
one or more players no longer have any realistic chance of winning.

Fred

Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
In message <1140023250....@z14g2000cwz.googlegroups.com>,

Ector <Ec...@mail.ru> writes:
>AFAIK, *every* player has some way to oust all other players - at
>least, the probability of this is greater than zero. Does this mean
>that ALL table-splitting deals are illegal?
>Anyway, how can a judge determine the EXACT number of VPs any player
>can get? When a player wants to deal for 1 VP, somebody would call a
>judge... and the judge should determine the minimal number he could
>deal for, doesn't he?

You're missing the point. The judge doesn't have to determine the EXACT
number of VPs any player can get. The judge has to use his judgement of
whether the player is playing to win (bearing in mind that players make
mistakes), and that the deal is - in his or her opinion - reasonable
enough that they don't feel obliged to block it at any appropriate point
in the future.

The judge is not required to create a cast-iron case against a player
such that it would stand up in a court of law - though most will feel
obliged to be able to justify their judgement if challenged.
(Potentially, they won't feel able to justify it there and then, since
they will have accurate knowledge that each player doesn't have - the
state of a given hand or uncontrolled region, for example.)

It's simply a judgement call. Is each player playing to win, or to
maximise VPs if not? And are they taking a reasonable cause of action
towards that goal?

--
James Coupe

Let's take a 4-player table (players A, B, C and D). Player A feels
that he is unable to get more than 1 VP and he proposes an 1-3 deal to
his grandprey, player C. Player D calls the judge, and the judge
determines that player A *can* get more than 1VP, so the deal would be
illegal. Then player B proposes a 2-2 deal to player C, and this time
the judge thinks the deal is legal. But player A immediately states,
that WITH THAT DEAL he's clearly unable to get more than 1VP, so he
again proposes his 1-3 deal to player C.
If the judge believes that with the 2-2 deal player A would really be
unable to get more than 1VP, should he call the not-yet-made 2-2 deal

deck without additional stealth sitting between two intercept decks

use your judgement. pretend like you are the player who wants to deal
for only 1 vp. look at his hand, have a quick flip through his library
to get a feel for the deck, try and gauge his playing ability.

then, think reasonably about whether you think that player could get
more than 1 vp without the deal, playing in a reasonable manner, knowing
only what that player knows.

there is no percentage, there is no right or wrong. sure, with luck this
guy might draw all the right cards while everyone else gets crap and he
could end up sweeping. but is it reasonable to think that here and now,
at the time of the deal?

it all depends on the situation. if you can't make a reasonable
judgement as to whether he could get more or not, get an assistant
judge, or trust the player, or something. but, you know, make a
judgement. don't dick around going "ohh, but i think he has a 33% chance
of more, and i call the reasonable level to be 35%, so therefore he can
make the deal...". Get real. there is no possible way you could
practicably apply number to these sorts of situations.

Ector, I see your struggle, and I appreciate it. I have been there.
I've spent many hours trying to understand the play to win rules, and
trying to become a better judge. Sit back, relax, and allow me to
teach you what I know. :)

If you want to skip to the really good part, here's the thread to read:
http://tinyurl.com/acvaw

It goes to the heart of your issue: how does a judge define
"reasonable?" Elsewhere in that thread, it also touches on assigning
numbers to "reasonable," if it would improve consistency of rulings
across all judges, and why it makes no sense to even attempt to assign
a number to it (since "reasonable" isn't a probability, it's a risk
analysis.)

Remember that all of this discussion stems from this rule:

Players are expected to behave in a respectful and sportsmanlike manner
at all times. (Tournament Rule 2.3.)

That includes more than just "play to win." Play to win is defined as:

1) You must try to get a GW. If you already have a GW, you can play
however you choose (give away other VPs, try to get more VPs, doesn't
matter.)
2) If you don't have a reasonable chance at a GW, you must try to
maximize your VPs.
3) If you don't have a reasonable chance at any VPs, you can earn 0 VPs
in whatever manner you choose (including self-oust, walling up, cross
table whatever, etc.)

There have already been some revelant discussions on these points. The
link above is a good starting point.

Here is one regarding Play to Win in the finals:
http://tinyurl.com/dtql6

And another one that clarifies Play to Win in the finals:
http://tinyurl.com/8ptfz

To address your specific question above, you should remember another
thing: an illegal deal can be proposed and accepted. Talk is cheap.
The judge only needs to step in when an actual illegal play occurs.

Let's break down your example above:

> Player A feels that he is unable to get more than 1 VP and
> he proposes an 1-3 deal to his grandprey, player C.

Remember it's not "unable to get more than 1 VP." It is, "no
reasonable chance to get more than 1 VP," as defined by a risk analysis
of "reasonable" by the judge. The player's opinion of "reasonable"
will also likely sway the judge.

> Player D calls the judge, and the judge determines that
> player A *can* get more than 1VP, so the deal would be illegal.

Remember it's not "can get more than 1 VP," it's "has a reasonable
chance to get more than 1 VP," where "reasonable" can include the
consequences of failure (i.e. risk analysis.)

For purposes of example, let's say that the judge determines that A
could reasonably get more than 1 VP. In that case, the deal would be
illegal - you're right. BUT - the judge should not announce that
information to the table. The judge should let A know privately that
it's an unenforceable deal (so that if A was planning on transferring
out later, he'll know that it would be illegal.) I clearly recall a
thread on this topic where LSJ was quite illuminating, but
unfortunately I couldn't find it (and I did look!) If anyone else can
scrounge it up, please do.

The judge should also make it clear to everyone at the table that they
must play to win. You can tell D that if A actually does something
that's not play to win, then he can call you over again.

> <snip the rest of the example>

> Wouldn't this be extremely ridiculous?

Yes, which is why the judge need not (and should not) announce to the
table if the deal is legal or not. The only thing the judge should
actively prohibit is anything that's not play to win. Dealmaking is
just talk.

> Please, tell me, where do you get such omniscient judges?
> Unfortunately, I'm unable to make such decisions in any reasonable time.

Of course you can. When in doubt, let the player decide his own fate,
unless it's clearly not play to win.

I hope this helps. I welcome more discussion on this interesting topic
(IMO.) I especially welcome any corrections, if I've made any
mistakes, though I feel confident about the accuracy of everything I
posted. :)

Cheers,

Ira

Surely the main point of making a 1 - 2 - 2 split would either
i) you only need 1 VP to quailfy for the final and so in the wider

jibbajibba wrote:
> Surely the main point of making a 1 - 2 - 2 split would either
> i) you only need 1 VP to quailfy for the final and so in the wider
> tournament sense you are PTW

That's called "out of game consideration", and doesn't factor into
deciding if something is play to win (also that category: players'
rankings, win records, body odor, command of the common language,
etc.)

> iii) you are lying and intend to sweep the table but need to get a
> combo engine running that will take 3 turns to set up.

The discussion of PTW with regard to deals is always about honoring
the deal when the time come to honor it and honoring it involves
doing something that is not in and of itself playing to win (if the
activity were in and of itself playing to win, then the presence or
absence of a deal has no bearing).

You are free to make any deal at all, so long as every game activity
is in and of itself play to win (i.e., you break your deal whenever it
conflicts with play to win).

> If after this sort of 'deal' the judge took me to one side and said
> that I was in breach of the rules I would point out, in private, that I
> have no intention to stick to the deal but was just maximizing my
> chance to win by removing a threat from 2 of my opponents. Since no
> deals are binding in the rules and the Judge lacks the power to read my
> mind he can't know if I am lying to him or lying to the other members
> of my cabal so how can he rule either way?

He doesn't. The judgment only comes in at the time where a player
seeks to honor a deal instead of playing to win.

It is legal to honor the deal if making the deal (to honor it) was an
example of playing to win at the time the deal was made.

That is, it is legal to honor a legally-made deal.

It is legal to break a deal.

It is legal to make an illegal-to-honor deal, but then you'd have to
break it when it came time to play to win vs. keep the deal.

Messages.Author: ira...@gmail.com
Messages.Body:
> So what's the difference? Player A now knows that his deal is going to
> be illegal, but player C doesn't know this, right? So player A can
> break the deal, but cannot give up through it, and that's all?

Yes, that is my understanding.

> If player A doesn't want to be a dealbreaker, he would refuse his
> proposal, and everyone would understand that the deal wasn't legal.

That sounds about right.

I'd say the solution to your dilemma is that the judge should very
rarely prevent a player from following their desired course of action
regarding play to win. There may be some cases of a very spiteful
player transferring out, or collusion, but most of the time, I think
players will choose to play to win. If you ask player A, "Do you
really think you don't have any reasonable chance at getting more than
1 VP?" And he says, "Yes," then if I were the judge, I'd probably let
him make the deal.

If I prevent the deal, he can just play poorly instead. And I could
try to prevent that as a judge, too, but it gets very difficult to
enforce. So, as a judge, I would remind the players of the play to win
rule, ensure they understood it, and then generally let them play how
they desire.

Remember the basis for the play to win rule is the sportsmanship rule,
so let that guide you and the players, too.

It sounds to me like you're talking about a situation where players
honestly want to follow the rules; if you're actually talking about a
situation where the judge believes A and C are colluding, then I would
be much more strict as the judge, and more willing to disallow such
deals. Fortunately, I haven't been put in that situation. :)

Finally, in your specific example, if, as the judge, I was going to be
bold enough to deem a deal from A illegal, it's likely that I'd also
prevent B from making a deal that gave away the game. And regarding
A's offer to hand the game to C, you're never obligated to accept a
deal by Play to Win, because deals can be broken.

I hope this helps,

Ira

In message <1140349498.4...@g44g2000cwa.googlegroups.com>,

Cooper <wouter...@gmail.com> writes:
>Wouldnt it be possible to grant 0.5 GW for the ones with 2 VP's in a
>2-2-1 (or 2-2 for a 4playertable) split?

It would, but it re-introduces problems of its own.

One of the reasons[0] the GW rule was introduced was the problem of e.g.
combat decks deciding to split a table. The problem was particularly
pronounced in combat decks when they sat next to each other, but other
decks could benefit from the same situation.

The textbook situation is to have two combat decks sitting next to each
other which will mutually annihilate each other. No VP each. So they
decide to nuke the other three players together, and one of the combat
players gets 3VP and the other gets 2VP.

Prior to the GW rule, the difference between 3VP and 2VP was 1VP - which
is not a lot, in the grand scheme of 10 or 15 possible VPs. In the GW
world, however, one of the players gets 1GW and the other gets 0GW.
Which with only two or three GWs available is a significant difference,
meaning that each player wants to be on the 3VP end of the split,
meaning that skilled players build decks which won't get into that
situation or which can rule it like a God if they do. i.e. they design
and play for the game win first and foremost, rather than thinking
"Well, even if I sit next to another combat deck, I can still get 2VP so
it's still pretty good."

Going to a situation where they can say "Well, I'll get half a VP and
you'll get half a VP and that's just fine" (on a 4 player table) or
where they decide to oust someone cross-table and then split the other 2
each is therefore problematic. I'd be wary of such a rule change as a
result.

[0] There were a number of inter-related and complex reasons at the
time, but this is one of the more important. I'm not saying it's the
only reason, though!



to, using normal quotation techniques - addition of > at the start of

>I think it is VERY possible that one of these combat decks
>will win the game, even if they are next to eachother. That would mean
>that making a deal for a 2-2-1 split would be illegal, and therefor
>cannot be followed upon.

Experience shows otherwise, as does a little application of player
psychology.

The evidence of two combat decks sitting next to each other mutually
annihilating each other in pre-GW days is legion, forcing the relevant
table splits. I think you'll need to do a LOT of work to show that this
doesn't happen that isn't just a one line "I think it is VERY possible".

You also need to understand that the play-to-win rule does not allow a
judge to intervene and educate players about the fuller impact of their
actions. A judge cannot, for example, point out a way for a player to
get a GW that they miss. A judge cannot legislate for mistakes, poor
play or similar.

However, in a situation where I can get 0VP (mutual annihilation) as has
been shown by multiple situations throughout Jyhad history, or I can get
1 GW (but it's very, very unlikely) or I can aim for a solid 0.5 GW, a
judge does not necessarily have to stop you getting the 0.5 GW if the 1
GW is going to be exceedingly hard to get. Nor can the judge force you
to make a deal - which may be the only sensible way you can get a 1 GW
(by allowing a player in a losing position to maximise VPs, say).

Further, if mutual annihilation is likely, a player who could get 2 VPs
out of a deal with you (where you net 3 VPs) may refuse to do so if he
knows he can get 0.5 GW. At which point, if you need the help, you may
well be in a situation where the 0.5 GW is the much better option for
you (the 1 GW being a remote possibility).



> unlikely" is up to the judge. If it is really "very very unlikely" he
> shouldnt stop you. If it is however "unlikely but still rather
> possible" the judge should stop you.

I think it's very rare that the judge should step in and force a player
to play a certain way, if the player confirms that he's playing to win,
where playing to win is defined as:

1) Get a GW.
2) If you don't have a reasonable chance at a GW, get as many VPs as
possible.
3) If you don't have a reasonably chance to gain any more VPs, get zero
more VPs however you want.

> Imagine a similar situation. 3rd round of tournament. I need 2 VP's to
> be certain of a place in the finals. I can make an easy losing deal for
> my 2 VP's. I am not allowed however, because there is still a
> reasonable chance that i get the GW. Even if going for that chance
> would decrease my chances of getting in the finals.

You should not consider the finals, correct. But, remember that
"reasonable" includes risk analysis. That is, you can consider what
happens in the failure states. If you say, "I have a small chance to
get a GW. If I go for it and fail, I'll get zero VPs. OR, I could
take 2 VPs practically guaranteed." In that situation, you might not
have a "reasonable" chance at a GW because the consequences of failure
are so high.

Therefore, a player in that situation could take the 2 VP deal, and I
think a good judge would not prevent them from doing so (assuming the
player is only considering the consequences of that game, and not
thinking about getting into the finals.)

Regarding playing to get into the finals, I think that problem can be
avoided in many cases by not sharing the results of already completed
games. Sure, it's not completely secret, but you can minimize problems
by not publicly announcing, "If you get 2 VPs, you're guaranteed to get
into the finals!"

Also, to elaborate on the example, let's say the player has a small
chance to get a GW, but if he goes for it and fails, he still gets 2
VPs. In this case, a good judge would rule that it's unreasonably to
give up the GW just yet. The failure states matter.

Finally, because I think the link below is one of the most illuminating
play-to-win discussions provided by LSJ, and it includes information
that many people haven't internalized, I'm including it again:

http://tinyurl.com/acvaw

Ira

> Meaning i can read "reasonable chance" as "small, unlikely, but none

> 80-20 percentages (doesnt have to relate to VTES)
> i would say the "80" part is likely to happen, the "20" part is
> unlikely to happen.
> But i would also say that the 20 part is still a very reasonable
> chance.

This is a great example, Wouter! Consider these two cases:

1) You pay me $1. 20% of the time you win $100. 80% you get nothing.
I would say that is a "reasonable" risk.

2) You pay me $1. 20% of the time, you win $100. 80% you DIE. I
would say that is NOT a "reasonable" risk.

In both situations, the positive outcome is the same (win $100.) But
one is reasonable and the other is not, because of the failure states.

That is why risk analysis is necessary, and you can't simply assign a
numerical value to "reasonable." It depends what the other outcomes
are.

> another (say 1 VP) should be ranked higher than getting 4 VP's but
> losing both games?

We're just talking about personal opinions here? In my personal
opinion, I think the current tournament rules regarding GWs, VPs, and
TPs are excellent, and do not need to be modified.
